genZNote: No peptidoglycan, no independent metabolism, no standard culture — it's basically an intracellular freeloader that also happens to be the most common bacterial STI on the planet.

morphology.shape: Small coccoid/spherical elementary and reticulate bodies
morphology.size: Elementary body ~0.3 µm; reticulate body ~0.5-1 µm
morphology.oxygenRequirement: Obligate intracellular — relies entirely on host cell ATP (an 'energy parasite'); not classically categorized by free-living oxygen requirement
morphology.notes: Lacks a classical peptidoglycan layer (no muramic acid) despite having a Gram-negative-type outer membrane; does not reliably Gram stain

habitat.naturalHabitat: Obligate intracellular — infects columnar/transitional epithelial cells of the genital tract, conjunctiva, and respiratory tract
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Cannot survive or replicate outside host cells; the elementary body is the environmentally stable, infectious extracellular form

microscopy.stain: Giemsa or iodine staining of intracytoplasmic inclusions (historical); immunofluorescence with fluorescent antibody
microscopy.appearance: Intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies within infected epithelial cells

culture.media: McCoy cell culture (required — cannot be grown on standard bacteriologic media)
culture.growthCharacteristics: Obligate intracellular; biphasic developmental cycle (infectious elementary body → metabolically active reticulate body → new elementary bodies)
culture.colonyMorphology: Not applicable — forms intracellular inclusions rather than colonies

identificationClues: Obligate intracellular organism — cannot be cultured on standard bacteriologic media; requires cell culture (McCoy cells) if culture is attempted at all
Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) is the diagnostic gold standard on urine or genital swab specimens
Unique biphasic life cycle: infectious elementary body converts to a metabolically active reticulate body inside the host cell
Serovars A-C cause trachoma (leading infectious cause of blindness worldwide); D-K cause genital tract infection; L1-L3 cause lymphogranuloma venereum

diseases: Nongonococcal urethritis/cervicitis — the most common bacterial sexually transmitted infection
Pelvic inflammatory disease, which can lead to infertility and ectopic pregnancy
Trachoma (serovars A-C) — leading infectious cause of blindness worldwide
Neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia acquired during vaginal delivery
virulenceFactors: Obligate intracellular lifestyle evading extracellular immune defenses
Inhibition of phagosome-lysosome fusion within the host cell
Type III secretion system injecting effector proteins into host cells
clinicalImportance.transmission: Sexual contact (genital serovars); perinatal transmission during vaginal delivery (neonatal conjunctivitis/pneumonia); trachoma serovars spread via direct/fomite contact with eye or nose secretions, often facilitated by flies in endemic areas
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: The most commonly reported bacterial sexually transmitted infection in many countries; often asymptomatic, which contributes to ongoing transmission and delayed diagnosis of complications like PID and infertility
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: NAAT has replaced culture and antigen testing as the diagnostic standard due to far superior sensitivity; co-testing for Neisseria gonorrhoeae is routine given frequent co-infection

examFacts.gramReaction: Not Gram-typed — obligate intracellular, lacks classical peptidoglycan
examFacts.importantDisease: Most common bacterial STI; leading infectious cause of blindness (trachoma, serovars A-C)
examFacts.importantTest: Nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) of urine or genital swab
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: An obligate intracellular 'energy parasite' with a unique elementary-body/reticulate-body life cycle, diagnosed by NAAT rather than culture
